annotations.keyFindings: High-performing departments had nurse-initiated antibiotic protocols, a sepsis champion on every shift and antibiotics near triage; low performers relied on physician orders and described crowding and night-time gaps.
annotations.limitations: Emergency departments only; six sites in one country; performance defined by one indicator.

annotations.keyFindings: Antibiotics within one hour ranged from 41 to 86 percent across nine hospitals, lower at night and weekends in every hospital.
annotations.limitations: Recognition time recorded differently between hospitals; no reasons examined.

annotations.keyFindings: Across 27 studies, crowding, unclear ordering responsibility and delayed antibiotic access were the most consistent barriers; nurse-initiated protocols, leadership and feedback the most consistent facilitators.
annotations.limitations: Few direct comparisons of high and low performers; night care rarely examined.

annotations.keyFindings: Median triage-to-antibiotic time fell from 94 to 58 minutes after nurse-initiated protocols, least at night and where nurses lacked confidence.

claims.text: High-performing emergency departments had nurse-initiated antibiotic protocols, a sepsis champion on every shift and antibiotics stocked near triage.
claims.passage: High-performing departments had nurse-initiated antibiotic protocols, a sepsis champion on every shift and antibiotics stocked near triage.
claims.interpretation: Candidate determinants to explore and contrast across the five sites.

claims.text: In one regional network, the share of patients receiving antibiotics within one hour ranged from 41 to 86 percent between hospitals and was lower at night everywhere.
claims.passage: The proportion of patients receiving antibiotics within one hour of recognition ranged from 41 to 86 percent between hospitals.
claims.interpretation: Variation of the size described locally is common; network data can select contrasting sites.

claims.text: Crowding, unclear responsibility for ordering and delayed access to antibiotics were the most consistent barriers across 27 studies.
claims.passage: Across 27 studies, the most consistent barriers were crowding, unclear responsibility for ordering antibiotics and delayed access to antibiotics
claims.interpretation: A starting codebook, to be tested against local accounts.

claims.text: Median time to antibiotics fell from 94 to 58 minutes after nurse-initiated protocols were introduced in four departments.
claims.passage: median time from triage to antibiotics fell from 94 to 58 minutes after the protocol started
claims.interpretation: Suggests one strategy to consider once determinants are known.

synthesis: Four retrieved records, a small yield. A multi-site study and a review of 27 studies agree on the main determinants: nurse-initiated protocols, a champion on every shift, antibiotics stocked near triage, leadership and feedback help; crowding, unclear responsibility for ordering and distant antibiotic stock hinder. Variation between hospitals of the size described locally is common and is worse at night. Few studies compare high and low performers directly or examine night care, which is what this question needs.
gradeRationale: Qualitative evidence from a multi-site study and a review with GRADE-CERQual ratings mostly moderate, consistent across settings; the quantitative records are non-randomised or descriptive. Moderate confidence in the main determinants; low for night-time care.
summary: Four retrieved records appraised; four claims recorded; overall certainty moderate for the determinants.
